2026-11-22-the-great-stink.title: The Great Stink
2026-11-22-the-great-stink.description: In 1858 the River Thames smelled so bad that Parliament nearly fled London. The sewer system built in response was based on a wrong theory of disease, and it saved more lives than almost any medicine of its century.
2026-11-22-the-great-stink.html:
The Great Stink

In the summer of 1858, London held its breath. It was one of the hottest summers anyone could remember, and the River Thames, the great artery of the richest city on Earth, had turned into something closer to an open sewer. The water was brown and thick. Along the banks, the mud baked in the sun and gave off a smell so overpowering that people walking across the bridges pressed handkerchiefs to their faces and hurried to the other side.

Inside the brand-new Houses of Parliament, which sat right on the river, the situation was becoming impossible. Workers hung curtains soaked in chloride of lime over the windows, hoping the chemical would mask the stench. It didn't. Members talked seriously about moving the business of government somewhere else, perhaps to Oxford, perhaps to Hampton Court, anywhere upwind. One day Benjamin Disraeli, then leader of the House of Commons, was seen leaving a committee room in a hurry, a handkerchief clamped to his nose, papers in his other hand.

The newspapers had a name for it within weeks. They called it the Great Stink.

What happened next is one of the great stories of engineering, and also one of the great ironies of science. Because the men who fixed London's sewage problem were acting on a theory of disease that was completely wrong. And yet they ended up saving more lives than almost any medical breakthrough of the nineteenth century.

A city drowning in its own waste

To understand how London got here, you have to picture what the city had become. In 1800, around one million people lived there. By the late eighteen-fifties, it was more like two and a half million, and still growing fast. Railways were pulling in workers from all over the country. Factories, tanneries, slaughterhouses and gasworks crowded along the river.

For centuries, Londoners had dealt with human waste in a simple way. It went into cesspits, brick-lined holes beneath houses and back yards. Men known as night-soil collectors would come and empty them, often selling the contents to farmers outside the city as fertiliser. It was unpleasant, but it more or less worked, as long as the city stayed a manageable size.

Then two things changed. The first was the flushing toilet. Water closets became fashionable in the first half of the century, and they sent far more liquid into cesspits than the old system was ever designed for. Cesspits overflowed into cellars and streets. The second change was well-meaning reform. Officials, convinced that the foul air rising from cesspits was itself a cause of disease, ordered that houses be connected to the existing sewers instead.

The problem was where those sewers went. London's old sewers had been built to carry rainwater, and almost all of them emptied straight into the Thames. So in trying to clean up the streets, the authorities had turned the river into the city's toilet. And that same river was where several private water companies drew the drinking water they piped into people's homes.

The invisible killer

Through the middle decades of the century, London was struck again and again by cholera. It was a terrifying disease. A healthy person could wake up feeling fine and be dead by nightfall, wracked by violent diarrhoea and dehydration. The outbreak of 1848 and 1849 killed around fourteen thousand people in London alone. Another, in 1853 and 1854, killed more than ten thousand.

Nobody knew what caused it. The dominant belief among doctors and officials was the miasma theory: the idea that diseases were spread by bad air, by poisonous vapours rising from rotting matter. If something smelled terrible, the reasoning went, it was probably making you ill. This wasn't a stupid idea. Filth and disease really did go together. But it pointed people at the wrong culprit.

A few people suspected otherwise. The most famous was a London physician named John Snow. In 1854, during an outbreak in Soho, Snow went door to door recording where the victims had lived. He plotted the deaths on a map, and they clustered tightly around a single public water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle, and the outbreak, which was already waning, subsided.

Snow also compared households supplied by two different water companies. One drew its water from the Thames downstream of the sewer outlets. The other had moved its intake upstream, to cleaner water. The death rate among customers of the first company was many times higher.

It was powerful evidence that cholera travelled through water, not air. But most of the medical establishment wasn't convinced. Snow died in 1858, the very summer of the Great Stink, with his theory still widely dismissed.

Eighteen days

So in June 1858, when Parliament finally decided to act, it did so for the wrong reason. Members weren't worried about contaminated drinking water. They were worried about the smell, because they believed the smell itself was deadly, and they were the ones breathing it.

For years, plans to fix London's drainage had been stuck in a swamp of committees, competing proposals and arguments over who would pay. Now, with the stench pouring through the windows, that resistance evaporated. A bill was rushed through Parliament in about eighteen days. It gave a body called the Metropolitan Board of Works the authority, and the borrowing power, to build a proper system. The initial budget was three million pounds, a staggering sum at the time.

The man who would build it was the Board's chief engineer, Joseph Bazalgette. He was a small, serious man with a famously large moustache, and he had already spent years drawing up plans that no one had been willing to fund. Now he had his chance.

The plan

Bazalgette's idea was elegant. Instead of trying to stop the old sewers from flowing toward the river, he would intercept them. He designed a series of huge new sewers that ran parallel to the Thames, on both the north and south banks, cutting across the old drains like a gutter catching water from a row of spouts. The intercepting sewers would collect everything and carry it eastward, away from the centre of the city, mostly using gravity, with the sewers sloping gently downhill by about two feet every mile.

Where gravity wasn't enough, giant steam-powered pumping stations would lift the sewage up so it could keep flowing. Two of those stations survive today and are worth seeing. Crossness, on the south side, and Abbey Mills, on the north, look less like industrial buildings than cathedrals, with ornate cast ironwork painted in bright colours. Abbey Mills was nicknamed the cathedral of sewage. The Victorians believed that public works should be beautiful, even the ones that handled waste.

At the end of the line, far to the east of the city, the sewage was released into the Thames on the outgoing tide, to be carried out toward the sea.

Altogether, the scheme involved around eighty miles of large intercepting sewers, fed by more than a thousand miles of smaller street sewers. Building it took something like three hundred million bricks.

Building for the future

Two decisions made Bazalgette's system last far longer than anyone at the time could have expected.

The first was about size. Bazalgette calculated how big each pipe needed to be, based on the population it would serve. Then, the story goes, he doubled it. His reasoning was that they would only get to do this once, and the city would keep growing. He was right. London's population today is more than three times what it was in his time, and much of his system is still in use.

The second decision was about materials. Bazalgette insisted on Portland cement, a relatively new product that set harder than traditional mortar and, crucially, could set underwater. It was more expensive, and many engineers didn't trust it. So Bazalgette imposed a strict testing regime, checking batch after batch for strength. The result was brickwork that has survived well over a century of constant use.

The project also changed the face of the city above ground. To carry the northern intercepting sewer through central London, Bazalgette built the Victoria Embankment, reclaiming land from the muddy foreshore of the Thames. Inside the embankment ran the sewer, and alongside it, a tunnel for the new underground railway, today part of the District and Circle lines. On top went a wide road and riverside gardens. Much of the elegant riverside walk that tourists enjoy today exists because of a sewer.

The proof

The main system opened in stages. The Prince of Wales officially started the engines at Crossness in 1865. Then, in 1866, cholera returned to London one last time.

This outbreak was revealing. Almost all of the deaths, roughly five and a half thousand of them, were concentrated in the East End, in an area served by a water company drawing from a part of the River Lea that had been contaminated. This was also one of the districts where Bazalgette's system had not yet been connected. Investigators, including the statistician William Farr, traced the outbreak to the water supply. Farr had once been a believer in miasma. The evidence changed his mind.

Once the eastern sections of the network were finished, cholera never seriously returned to London. Typhoid deaths fell too. Over the following decades, the theory that Snow had championed became mainstream, helped along by the work of scientists such as Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch, whose research on germs finally explained why. Koch identified the cholera bacterium itself in 1883.

So the Victorians built the right thing for the wrong reason. They wanted to remove a smell. By doing it, they removed sewage from the water people were drinking, and that is what stopped the dying.

Not quite a happy ending

The story has a darker coda. Bazalgette's system moved London's sewage away from the centre, but it didn't treat it. The raw waste still went into the Thames, just further east.

In 1878, a pleasure steamer called the Princess Alice, packed with day-trippers, collided with a much larger ship near the sewage outfalls and sank within minutes. Around six hundred and fifty people died. Many victims, survivors said, were overcome not only by the water but by the filth in it, because the disaster happened shortly after a release of untreated sewage. The tragedy added weight to calls to treat the waste rather than just dump it, and over the following decades treatment works were added to the system.

Bazalgette himself was knighted in 1875 and died in 1891. There is a modest memorial to him on the Victoria Embankment, the riverside wall that hides his greatest work. It carries a short Latin inscription meaning, roughly, "he put the river in chains."

The sewer, a century and a half later

Here's the remarkable part. Bazalgette's sewers are still the backbone of London's drainage today. But the city eventually outgrew even his doubled pipes. Because the old system combined rainwater and sewage in the same tunnels, heavy storms would overwhelm it, and the overflow, by design, spilled into the Thames. By the early twenty-first century, this was happening dozens of times a year, sending millions of tonnes of untreated sewage into the river.

London's answer was a modern descendant of Bazalgette's idea: the Thames Tideway Tunnel, nicknamed the super sewer. It runs for about twenty-five kilometres, mostly beneath the river itself, to catch overflow before it reaches the water. It came into full operation in 2025, more than a century and a half after the Great Stink.

It's a fitting end to the story. The engineers who built it were working with a far better understanding of disease and ecology than the Victorians had. But the basic logic, intercept the waste, carry it away, and build bigger than you think you need, came straight from a small man with a big moustache who was handed his chance by a very bad summer.

Sometimes the most important public health breakthrough isn't a new drug or a new theory. Sometimes it's a lot of bricks, laid in the right place, by someone who planned for the city that didn't exist yet.

2026-11-22-the-bubble.title: The Bubble, Japan's boom, bust and lost decades
2026-11-22-the-bubble.description: In the late 1980s, Japan looked set to overtake the United States, and the land under the Imperial Palace was said to be worth more than all of California. Then the bubble burst. How it inflated, why it popped, and why the recovery took more than thirty years.
2026-11-22-the-bubble.html:
The Bubble

On the twenty-ninth of December, 1989, the traders of the Tokyo Stock Exchange gathered for the last session of the year. It was a short day, and a happy one. The Nikkei, the index that tracks the biggest companies in Japan, closed at a little under thirty-nine thousand points, the highest it had ever been. It had roughly tripled in five years. That evening, across Tokyo, bankers and brokers celebrated in restaurants where a single meal could cost a month of an ordinary worker's wages, and some of them, by popular legend, ate sushi sprinkled with flakes of real gold.

Nobody in those restaurants knew that they were standing at the very top. Within three years, the market would lose more than half its value. Land prices would begin a slide that lasted well over a decade. Some of the most powerful banks in the world would collapse or be quietly rescued by the state. And that number, thirty-nine thousand, would not be seen again for thirty-four years, until February of 2024.

This is the story of Japan's bubble economy, one of the most spectacular financial manias in history, and of the long, strange aftermath that economists came to call the lost decades. It is a story about money, but also about pride, about institutions that could not admit a mistake, and about a whole generation that grew up in the shadow of a party they never got to attend.

Japan as number one

To understand the bubble, you have to understand how unstoppable Japan seemed in the nineteen-eighties.

In 1945, much of the country lay in ruins. Its cities had been firebombed, two of them destroyed by atomic weapons, and its industry was shattered. Over the next few decades, it pulled off what became known as the Japanese economic miracle. Through the fifties and sixties, the economy grew at around ten percent a year, a pace almost unheard of for a country of its size. By the late sixties, Japan had become the second-largest economy in the free world.

And it did not stop. Japanese cars, cameras, televisions and electronics conquered global markets. Toyota, Honda, Sony, Panasonic and Nikon became household names in every rich country on Earth. Japanese factories were held up as models of efficiency and quality. Japanese management, with its lifetime employment, its company loyalty and its long-term thinking, was studied in business schools across America and Europe.

In 1979, the Harvard sociologist Ezra Vogel published a book with a title that captured the mood. It was called Japan as Number One. By the mid-eighties, many Americans were genuinely worried that Japan was about to overtake them, buying up their companies and their landmarks, and leaving the United States behind. Popular films and novels were full of Japanese corporations as the powers of the future. It seemed only a matter of time.

But there was a problem. Japan's export success had produced enormous trade surpluses, especially with the United States. Japan was selling far more to America than it was buying, and Washington was losing patience.

The Plaza Accord and the flood of money

On the twenty-second of September, 1985, the finance ministers of five major economies, the United States, Japan, West Germany, France and Britain, met at the Plaza Hotel in New York. They agreed to work together to bring down the value of the American dollar, which had become very strong, against the other major currencies. The deal became known as the Plaza Accord.

It worked, perhaps too well. Before the agreement, one dollar bought around two hundred and forty yen. By early 1988, it bought only about one hundred and twenty-five. In under three years, the yen had roughly doubled in value against the dollar.

For Japanese exporters, this was a shock. A car that earned a certain number of dollars in America now brought home far fewer yen. Japan slipped into a short recession, which the Japanese press named the high-yen slump. Factories worried about losing their markets. Politicians worried about unemployment.

So the government and the Bank of Japan, the country's central bank, did what governments usually do in that situation. They tried to stimulate the economy at home. The government was also under international pressure, including from an influential official report in 1986, to shift the economy away from exports and towards domestic spending. The Bank of Japan cut interest rates repeatedly, until by early 1987 its main lending rate stood at two and a half percent, the lowest it had been in decades. And then, crucially, it left rates there for more than two years.

At the same time, Japan's financial system was being deregulated. Banks that had long been tightly controlled were suddenly allowed to compete more freely, and they were losing their best corporate customers, big companies that could now raise money directly from the markets. Looking for new borrowers, the banks turned to property developers, smaller firms and anyone with land to offer as security.

Cheap money, eager lenders and a country convinced of its own destiny. All the ingredients were in place.

The bubble years

What followed was one of the most extraordinary booms the modern world has seen.

It started with land. Japan is a mountainous country, and usable flat land has always been precious. There was a long-standing belief, almost an article of faith, that land prices in Japan only ever went up. Banks lent against land as collateral, and as land prices rose, the collateral was worth more, so the banks lent more, and the borrowers used the money to buy more land, which pushed prices higher still. It was a loop, and for a few years it seemed to have no end.

Prices in central Tokyo became almost surreal. Some plots in the Ginza shopping district changed hands at prices equivalent to well over a hundred thousand dollars per square metre, about the size of a small table. And there was a famous calculation, repeated endlessly at the time and still quoted today, that the land under the Imperial Palace in the middle of Tokyo, a little over a square kilometre of gardens and moats, was worth more than all the real estate in the state of California. Whether the figure was precisely right hardly mattered. That people could say it with a straight face tells you everything.

The stock market followed. In 1987, the government began selling shares in the national telephone company, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone, known as N T T. Ordinary families queued to buy. Within a couple of months, the share price had more than doubled, and for a time N T T was valued as the most valuable company on Earth. By the end of the decade, Japanese firms made up most of the world's largest companies by stock market value, and the Tokyo market as a whole was, by some measures, worth more than the American one.

Japanese companies, flush with money, joined in the speculation. There was even a word for it, zaitech, a blend of the Japanese for finance and the English word technology. Manufacturing firms found that they could make more money trading shares and property than by making things.

And the money flowed abroad. In 1989, Sony bought the Hollywood studio Columbia Pictures. The same year, the Mitsubishi Estate company bought a controlling stake in the owner of Rockefeller Center, one of the most famous buildings in New York. Americans reacted with something close to panic, as if a piece of their national identity had been sold. Japanese buyers acquired luxury hotels, golf courses, including the celebrated Pebble Beach in California, and art. In 1987, a Japanese insurance company paid a record price for one of Van Gogh's paintings of sunflowers. In 1990, a Japanese paper magnate paid more than eighty million dollars for Van Gogh's Portrait of Doctor Gachet, at the time the highest price ever paid for a painting at auction.

Life in Tokyo during these years had a giddy quality. Taxis were famously hard to find late at night, and people waved banknotes in the street to attract one. Companies threw lavish parties for their employees and recruited graduates with overseas trips and expensive gifts. Golf club memberships were bought and sold like shares, some of them for prices equal to a house. It felt, to many people, as if Japan had simply discovered a better way to run an economy, and the rest of the world would have to catch up.

The pop

By the end of the decade, the authorities had become alarmed. Ordinary salaried workers could no longer dream of buying a home in or near Tokyo. Prices had detached from anything that rents or profits could justify. Something had to give.

In late 1989, a new governor took charge of the Bank of Japan. His name was Yasushi Mieno, and he made it clear that he intended to deflate the bubble. The bank had already begun raising its main rate earlier that year. Under Mieno, it kept going. Within about fifteen months of the first increase, the rate had risen from two and a half percent to six percent. In the spring of 1990, the Ministry of Finance also ordered banks to restrict the growth of their lending for property.

The stock market turned first. In the very first trading days of 1990, the Nikkei began to fall, and it kept falling. By the late summer of 1992, it had lost more than half its value from that December peak. Land prices followed more slowly, but for far longer. They fell year after year, through the nineties and into the two-thousands. By some estimates, commercial land in Japan's largest cities eventually lost more than eighty percent of its peak value.

Some of the trophy purchases abroad became symbols of the reversal. Pebble Beach was sold again within a couple of years, at a heavy loss. The company that owned Rockefeller Center filed for bankruptcy protection in 1995. The famous Van Gogh portrait disappeared from public view, reportedly sold off quietly after its buyer's business ran into trouble.

At first, many people in Japan assumed this was simply a correction. The economy had always bounced back before. But there was something buried underneath the falling prices that would turn a crash into a decades-long malaise.

The banks that would not admit it

Remember the loop that drove the boom. Banks lent money against land, and land prices kept rising. Now the loop ran in reverse. Land prices fell, so the collateral behind countless loans was suddenly worth far less than the loans themselves. Borrowers could not repay. And the banks were sitting on enormous losses.

In a healthy financial system, a bank in that position would admit the losses, write off the bad loans, raise new capital or fail, and the economy would take a painful hit and then move on. That is not what happened in Japan.

Instead, for years, the banks, and the regulators who oversaw them, preferred to pretend. Bad loans were rolled over, again and again, so that struggling borrowers could keep paying interest and nobody would have to admit that the money was gone. Companies that should have gone bankrupt were kept alive on fresh credit. Economists later called them zombie firms, companies that were not quite alive and not quite dead, occupying markets, workers and capital that healthier businesses could have used.

There were reasons for this, not all of them cynical. Japanese business culture placed great value on long relationships between banks and the companies they served. Admitting the full scale of the losses risked a panic. And many people sincerely believed that if everyone waited a little longer, land prices would recover and the problem would solve itself. But land prices did not recover. The bad debts grew. And the waiting went on for most of a decade.

The reckoning finally came in the autumn of 1997. In November of that year, Japan suffered a run of failures that shook the country. Hokkaido Takushoku, one of the country's largest commercial banks, collapsed, the first failure of a major Japanese bank since the war. And then came Yamaichi Securities, one of the four great brokerage houses of Japan, a firm with a history of a hundred years. Yamaichi had been hiding enormous losses off its books. When it announced that it was shutting down, its president appeared at a press conference and broke down in tears, bowing deeply and pleading that his employees were not to blame, that the fault lay with the management. The image of that sobbing executive was broadcast across the country, and for many people it became the moment they understood that the old certainties were over.

The following year, the government nationalised two of the country's big long-term credit banks, the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan and the Nippon Credit Bank, institutions that had once helped finance the postwar miracle. Over the following years, the remaining large banks were forced through mergers and recapitalisation, and a great deal of public money went into propping up the system.

Deflation and the lost generation

By the end of the nineties, Japan faced a problem that most economists had only read about in history books. Prices were falling. Not just the prices of shares and land, but the prices of ordinary goods in the shops.

That might sound like good news. Who would not want things to get cheaper? But persistent deflation is quietly corrosive. If people expect prices to be lower next year, they have a reason to put off buying things. Companies, seeing weak demand, hold back on investment and wages. Debts become heavier in real terms, because the money you owe stays the same while your income shrinks. The economy can settle into a low, grinding stagnation that is very hard to escape.

The Bank of Japan cut its interest rate to essentially zero in 1999, and in 2001 it became the first major central bank in the modern era to try what is now called quantitative easing, creating new money to buy financial assets in the hope of reviving lending and spending. These policies were controversial, and critics, including a Princeton economist named Ben Bernanke, argued that the bank was being far too timid. Remember that name. It comes back later in this story.

For ordinary people, the most painful effects were often felt in work. Japan's postwar system of lifetime employment protected the people who already had jobs. Companies tried hard not to fire their existing staff. Instead, they stopped hiring. For roughly a decade, from the early nineties to the mid two-thousands, Japanese graduates faced what came to be called the employment ice age. Young people who would once have walked into secure careers with a single company found themselves in temporary and part-time work, often for years, sometimes for good. Because Japanese companies traditionally hired mostly fresh graduates, missing that first chance could follow a person for the rest of their working life.

Many in that generation are now in their forties and fifties. Some never married or had children, often for economic reasons. Their story is one of the hidden costs of the bubble, paid by people who were children when the champagne was flowing in the restaurants of the Ginza.

The long road back

Recovery, when it came, came slowly and unevenly.

In the early two-thousands, the government of Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi pushed the banks, at last, to clean up their bad loans, and by the middle of the decade the banking system was finally on firmer ground. The economy grew modestly. Then came the global financial crisis of 2008, and Japan, heavily dependent on exports, was hit hard once again.

In 2012, Shinzo Abe returned as prime minister with a programme that became known as Abenomics. It combined government spending, structural reforms and, above all, an enormous expansion of money creation by the Bank of Japan under its new governor, Haruhiko Kuroda. The bank bought government bonds and other assets on a vast scale, and in 2016 it even pushed one of its key interest rates below zero. The aim was to break the deflationary mindset once and for all and to get prices and wages rising again.

For years, the results were mixed. The economy improved, unemployment fell, and companies became more profitable. But wages stayed stubbornly flat, and inflation kept falling short of the bank's target.

Then, in the early twenty-twenties, the world changed around Japan. A global surge in prices after the pandemic, a weaker yen and rising energy costs finally pushed Japanese inflation above two percent and kept it there. Workers began to win the biggest pay rises in decades. In February of 2024, the Nikkei finally closed above the record it had set on that December evening in 1989, thirty-four years and two months later. And in March of 2024, the Bank of Japan raised interest rates for the first time in seventeen years, bringing an end to its era of negative rates.

It was not a triumphant ending, exactly. Japan's population has been shrinking since around 2008, and it is one of the oldest societies on Earth. The country carries one of the largest government debts in the world relative to the size of its economy. But it did, at last, feel like the close of a very long chapter.

Lost decades, or something else?

So, were the decades really lost?

Some economists argue that the story is more complicated than the phrase suggests. Japan remained a rich, safe, orderly country throughout. Unemployment never reached the levels seen in many Western recessions. And if you measure growth per working-age person, rather than for the economy as a whole, Japan's performance in the two-thousands looks far less dismal, because much of its slow overall growth simply reflects an ageing population with fewer people of working age.

But the bubble and its aftermath left deep marks. A generation of young workers had their careers stunted. Trust in institutions was shaken. And the world learned some hard lessons, though it did not always learn them in time.

Here is the twist. When the global financial crisis struck in 2008, born of an American housing bubble fuelled by cheap credit and the conviction that property prices only went up, the man in charge of the United States central bank was Ben Bernanke. The same economist who had once criticised the Bank of Japan for its timidity. American and European policymakers, studying Japan's experience, moved much faster to rescue and recapitalise their banks, and to flood their economies with money. Whether they got everything right is still debated. But for a whole generation of central bankers, Japan's long struggle was the cautionary tale they were determined not to repeat. Economists even coined a word for the fear, Japanification.

In the end, perhaps the most lasting lesson of the Japanese bubble is the oldest one in finance. When everyone agrees that prices can only go up, when the land under one palace is said to be worth more than California, the party is usually closer to its end than anyone in the room can believe. And the cost of the hangover is often paid not by the people who were celebrating, but by the ones who arrived just after the music stopped.
